The announcement comes less than two weeks after Bristol Myers Squibb merged its research and development departments under one leader.
Bristol Myers Squibb’s top team continues to turn over, with CFO David Elkins announcing his departure less than two weeks after the pharma reorganized its R&D efforts as research head Robert Plenge announced his exit.
Elkins, current CFO and executive vice president, will relinquish his role on March 1, 2027, heading over to serve in the same title for the Coca-Cola Company in April. Elkins has held the top finance spot at the New Jersey-based pharma for more than seven years, joining the company via its $74 billion Celgene acquisition in 2019.
Kevin Dillon, who currently serves as a senior vice president and head of corporate finance and business operations at BMS, will take Elkins’ spot. Dillon has been with BMS since 2021 and spent 11 years at Pfizer before that.
In its announcement on Monday, BMS reaffirmed all components of its full year 2026 guidance that were shared on the company’s third quarter earnings call on Oct. 29. The pharma had raised its full year revenue forecast by 1%, from a range of $49-$50 billion to $49.75-$50.25 billion.
The new leadership announcement follows BMS’ decision to combine all R&D activities under one leader as Chief Research Officer Plenge prepares to leave by the end of the year. In his absence, BMS Chief Medical Officer and development head Cristian Massacesi will take the reins of the newly reorganized unit as pressure rises for the pharma to replenish its pipeline.

“Bringing research and development together will more closely connect our scientific and clinical expertise, sharpen portfolio decision-making and execution, and help us focus our resources on the opportunities with the greatest potential,” a BMS spokesperson told BioSpace at the time.
BMS has faced scrutiny for its pipeline efforts as the loss of exclusivity for blockbusters Opdivo and Eliquis looms. In 2025, Pfizer-partnered blood thinner Eliquis brought in $14.4 billion in global sales, while PD-1 checkpoint inhibitor Opdivo secured $10 billion—together accounting for about half of BMS’ entire $48.2 billion revenue.
Last month, analysts at BMO Capital Markets were underwhelmed with the company’s plans to prepare for the patent losses, with the key potential revenue replacements in BMS’ pipeline—Cobenfy, milvexian and admilparant—all holding a good amount of risk.
“Bringing research and development together as one organization is an important step in our work to position BMS for long-term growth,” BMS CEO Christopher Boerner said in a Nov. 12 announcement. “This combined R&D organization sets us up to attract and retain the best talent, build critical capabilities, and better integrate new technology.”

Photo: © Dreamstime.com
By Nils Roche
24 November 2026
The formation of container shipping’s first global liner alliance covering the north-south trades appears to be taking shape, The Loadstar has learned.
Container lines have traditionally treated the north-south trades as a set of separate marriages, on the assumption that the right partner depends on the trade.
However, according to sources in Asia, Maersk and Ocean Network Express (ONE) are working to develop a vessel-sharing agreement (VSA) covering the trades globally, rather than lane by lane.
The Loadstar has approached both carriers for comment but has yet to receive a formal response, and the form the VDSA would take is unclear.
Nonetheless, if confirmed it would be the first VSA of its kind – and its logic rests on ONE’s fleet, according to our provisional analysis below.
Their respective groupings, the Gemini Cooperation for Maersk and Premier Alliance for ONE, stop at east-west trades, while north-south has remained a patchwork of classic VSAs, where each carrier’s slots follow the ships it provides, and an agreement rarely covers more than two or three services.
Why not Hapag-Lloyd?
The obvious choice of partner for Maersk would be Hapag-Lloyd, its Gemini compatriot – but two things rule it out. The first is that CSAV owns 30% of it and sits in the shareholder pact that controls more than 70% of the carrier, so combining West Coast South America networks would join two incumbents serving the same Chilean and Peruvian exporters.
In that context, it is worth noting that Maersk and Hapag-Lloyd do not cooperate on any of their respective Asia-WC South America services – according to Xeneta’s eeSea liner database, Maersk operates two standalone strings, the AC1 and AC3, while Hapag-Lloyd’s three offerings are run in cooperation with MSC, HMM, and ONE.
Secondly, Hapag-Lloyd has relatively few ships coming – its orderbook is 19% of its fleet, the lowest of the eight largest carriers, on trades where Far East–Latin America capacity grew 14% in a year.
ONE poses fewer of those problems. On Far East–WC South America, for example, Linerlytica puts Maersk at 16.1% of weekly capacity and ONE at 9%; together a quarter of the trade, ahead of CMA CGM and MSC, from two carriers whose customers overlap less.
The ships are the point
ONE has the fleet those trades are moving towards. Alphaliner puts 36% of its operated capacity in ships of 10,000–15,100 teu, against 14% at Maersk. Of the 55 ships ONE has on order, 29 – representing 60% of the total 647,000 teu expected – fall in the same bracket.
Linerlytica puts the average ship on Far East–Latin America already at 10,032 teu.
However, only 10 of ONE’s 62 ships in that class currently work Latin American routes. Under the classic formula, ships buy slots, so tonnage converts directly into share. A global partner gives ONE’s newbuilds work without ONE building Latin American and African franchises alone. Maersk, whose next order according to Linerlytica is for 24,000 teu ships, would thus get mid-size capacity without ordering it.
What it will probably look like
“Global” may describe the scope more than the mechanics. North-south shippers pay for direct calls, Brazil reserves feeder legs for Brazilian-flag operators, and Mexico’s ports do little relay business. That points to core loops on one carrier’s ships where its fleet fits, and shared loops where the ship mix demands it, rather than a Gemini-style hub network.
The obstacles are real. Hapag-Lloyd sits alongside ONE in several of these consortia, so the deal means reordering them with Maersk’s own Gemini partner, and a quarter of Asia–WC South America capacity will interest regulators in Chile and Peru. And similar disentanglements will be necessary on other north-south trades: for example, Maersk continues to cooperate with CMA CGM on Asia-West Africa services. And although there were rumours that that cooperation might be coming to an end, they have subsided for now.
The quay question…
…will be where ONE’s 13,724 teu newbuilds are deployed in 2027.
The industry has assumed north-south partners must be chosen trade by trade. A Maersk–ONE framework tests a different premise: that the scarce input is the right ship, and a carrier holding them can be a partner almost everywhere.

Nuro is now testing Lucid Gravity robotaxis on public roads in the San Francisco Bay Area with nobody in the driver’s seat. The driverless testing starts in four Peninsula and South Bay cities, with a fleet of more than 100 Gravity SUVs delivered by Lucid for the program.
It’s the biggest step yet for the Uber-Nuro-Lucid partnership. But it comes with a quieter update: the public launch, originally promised for 2026, is now expected in Q1 2027.
Driverless in four cities, employee rides next
According to Nuro’s announcement , driverless testing covers Palo Alto, Mountain View, Los Altos, and Sunnyvale, with more Bay Area cities to follow next year. Uber employees will “soon” be able to ride in the driverless vehicles.
Nuro has run the Gravity robotaxis around the clock in the Bay Area and Houston since December 2025, but always with a safety driver. Before pulling the driver, the company says it ran no-vehicle-operator testing at its Las Vegas closed course, covering things like pedestrian encounters and right-of-way violations, plus large-scale simulation.
Advertisement - scroll for more content
Tilo Schwarz, Nuro’s head of the Nuro Driver, pointed out that driverless operation “isn’t new” for the company. That’s fair. Nuro has run driverless delivery pods in California since 2020. But this is its first time doing it with a passenger vehicle.
The regulatory pieces were already in place. As we reported in May , the California DMV extended Nuro’s driverless testing permit to the Lucid Gravity, and the CPUC followed with a drivered pilot permit for carrying passengers.
A short list, and Tesla isn’t on it
Nuro says it’s one of just six companies allowed to test without a driver on California roads. The DMV’s list, last updated November 5, confirms it: AutoMo, Nuro, Tensor, Waymo, WeRide, and Zoox.
Tesla isn’t one of them. Its “Tesla Robotaxi LLC” entity only holds a permit to test with a driver in California, and it has no deployment permit either.
Waymo, of course, is the benchmark. It already runs a paid, fully driverless service across much of the Bay Area, including the Peninsula and South Bay where Nuro is just now pulling its safety drivers.
The timeline keeps sliding
When Lucid, Nuro, and Uber announced the program in July 2025 , the plan was to launch “later next year” in a major US city. As recently as June, when Uber named Houston as the second market for mid-2027, the Bay Area launch was still slated for this year.
Now it’s Q1 2027. Not a huge slip, but it’s a slip.
The scale ambition has gone the other way. Uber’s purchase commitment grew from 20,000 vehicles to at least 35,000 Lucid vehicles with the Nuro Driver, starting with the Gravity and later Lucid’s upcoming midsize models. Uber will own and operate the cars with fleet partners, and they’ll only be available through the Uber app.
For context, Lucid delivered 3,806 vehicles in Q3 2026. At that pace, 35,000 robotaxis would take more than two years of Lucid’s entire output.
Electrek’s Take
This is real progress, and it deserves credit. Nuro got the permits, built a formal safety case, tested at a closed course, and only then took the driver out. That’s how it should be done, and it should be applauded, especially as some companies claim to lead in autonomy while being too chicken to get a permit in California.
But let’s keep it in perspective. Driverless testing in four suburban cities with a 100-car fleet is where Waymo was years ago. Waymo is already doing hundreds of thousands of paid rides a week, including in the same part of the Bay Area. Nuro and Uber aren’t catching up to Waymo in 2027.
The bigger question for me is Lucid. The partnership gives Lucid exactly the kind of volume it needs, and 35,000 vehicles is a big number for a company delivering under 4,000 cars a quarter.
If this program is successful, and that’s a big if, then it could really help Lucid get to its more affordable vehicle.

Ports America has appointed Craig Mygatt as its next chief executive, bringing a veteran of marine terminals, container shipping and infrastructure investment to the helm of the largest U.S. marine terminal operator and stevedore.
The Morristown, N.J.-based company said Mygatt will succeed Scott Anderson, who has served as interim CEO since July 2026 and will remain chairman of the board.
Craig Mygatt
Mygatt brings more than 35 years of industry experience and most recently served as an operating partner at Macquarie Asset Management ( MQG.AX ). He previously led Ceres Terminals from 2020 to 2023, overseeing a North American terminal and stevedoring business spanning containers, cruise, roll-on/roll-off and breakbulk operations.
Before Ceres, Mygatt spent more than three decades at Maersk (OTC: AMKBY ) in roles including corporate planning and North American inland operations. He became CEO of SeaLand in 2014, with responsibility for Maersk Line’s operations across North American and Latin American trade lanes.
“Craig is a proven leader with deep experience on both the terminal and the carrier sides of our industry,” Anderson said in a release. “His track record of safe, reliable operations and strong customer relationships makes him the right leader for Ports America’s next chapter.”
Ports America operates at more than 70 locations across more than 30 U.S. ports, providing container, roll-on/roll-off, breakbulk, military and cruise services.
The company handled approximately 19 million twenty-foot equivalent units in 2024. By comparison, Drewry’s latest global review places PSA International first with 69.9 million TEUs in equity-adjusted throughput in 2025.
Mygatt said his priorities would center on the company’s people and operating relationships. “I look forward to working alongside our team, customers, labor partners and port authorities to build on that foundation, with safety and service at the center of everything we do,” he said.
Mygatt will take over as Ports America advances major development initiatives on the Gulf and East coasts. The company and Geneva-based Mediterranean Shipping Co.’s Terminal Investment Limited are private-sector partners in the Louisiana International Terminal, which received its federal construction permit in August. In Baltimore, Ports America Chesapeake’s Seagirt Marine Terminal is preparing for additional double-stack rail traffic through a $42 million intermodal expansion scheduled to begin construction in October and reach completion in 2028.
A source told FreightWaves that Ports America has been looking at expansion overseas including in Panama, where longtime operator CK Hutchison ( 0001.HK ) of Hong Kong was recently ousted. Maersk’s APM Terminals received the temporary operating assignment for Balboa, on the Pacific side of the Panama Canal. MSC’s TIL unit received the corresponding assignment for Cristobal, on the Atlantic side. Both arrangements were approved for up to 18 months in February 2026.
Why It Matters: The appointment puts an executive with experience on both sides of the ship-to-shore relationship—ocean carriers and terminal operators—in charge of a major U.S. cargo-handling network.

BYD launched the third-generation Tang, a large, high-tech five-seat flagship electric SUV, starting at under $30,000 in China.
BYD third-gen Tang EV prices and specs
The new third-gen Tang is positioned below the Great Tang, or “Da Tang” as it’s called in China, BYD’s larger seven-seat flagship SUV in its Dynasty lineup.
BYD held a launch event for its new flagship five-seat electric SUV on Tuesday. The third-gen Tang is available in three variants: standard Premium, Laser Premium, and Laser Flagship.
All versions come standard with rear-wheel drive (RWD), but buyers can upgrade the Laser Flagship model with an optional all-wheel-drive (AWD) steer-by-wire package for an extra 20,000 yuan ($3,000).
Advertisement - scroll for more content
Prices for the standard Tang Premium start at 187,900 yuan, or about $28,000, significantly lower than its pre-sale price of 225,000 yuan ($34,000).
The Laser Premium and Laser Flagship models start at 207,900 yuan and 219,900 yuan, respectively, also well below the pre-sale price.
All versions use BYD’s second-generation Blade LFP Batteries. RWD models use a single 402 hp (300kW) electric motor, delivering CLTC ranges of 453 miles (730 km) for the base Premium model and 528 miles (850 km) for the Laser Premium and Laser Flagship versions.
Upgrading to the dual-motor AWD powertrain bumps power to 690 hp (515 kW) and delivers a CLTC range of up to 478 miles (770 km).
The optional AWD steer-by-wire package adds a premium touch with a drive-by-wire digital chassis, reclining driver’s seats, a 35.4″ integrated Star Ring display screen, and intelligent electric all-wheel-drive.
BYD third-generation Tang EV interior (Source: Lu Tian)
All versions feature BYD’s Flash Charging tech, enabling it to charge from 10% to 80% in five minutes, or nine minutes for a full recharge (10% to 97%).
Inside, the flagship SUV adopts a five-seat layout and is packed with huge digital screens and premium extras.
The third-gen Tang features two giant screens: a 35.4″ integrated Star Ring display and a 30″ panoramic theater screen.
BYD third-generation Tang electric SUV interior (Source: Lu Tian)
BYD said the five-seat setup opens up interior space for passengers, claiming the new Tang SUV has the largest front trunk (frunk) in its class at 205L. It also offers a generous 1,000 mm of legroom for rear passengers.
The flagship electric SUV is equipped with BYD’s latest tech and other features, including its God’s Eye B laser-assisted driving system with DiPilot300 and Disus-A dual-chamber intelligent air suspension body control system.
BYD’s God’s Eye B uses a roof-mounted LiDAR to support ADAS features such as city navigation assist, high-speed navigation assist, and all-scenario parking assist.
The third-gen Tang also has BYD’s new high-speed tire blowout stability system, which can keep the vehicle stable and in its lane at up to 112 mph (180 km/h).

ATCC opened its Centennial Biomanufacturing Center in Manassas, Virginia, adding a U.S. site that will make, store and ship biological materials used in medical research and product development. The nonprofit says it invested more than $55 million in the project, with additional funding from federal and state grants.
What’s Related
The 50,000-square-foot center is at ATCC’s headquarters in Prince William County’s Innovation Park. The organization, formally known as the American Type Culture Collection, expects the expansion to create up to 75 full-time jobs .
The center will also check the identity and properties of the materials it makes before sending them to researchers. ATCC says it built the facility to handle large orders and increase production when demand rises, including during public health emergencies.
From production to shipping
ATCC supplies cell lines and other biological reference materials to government agencies, universities , and companies. Researchers use those materials as a common starting point so they can compare results across labs or repeat an experiment using the same kind of sample.
With production and storage at the same site, ATCC can prepare materials for shipment from the facility where they’re made and checked. ATCC says it will use secure handling procedures and temperature-controlled shipping to keep the materials in usable condition during distribution.
“When public health threats emerge, the nation's response depends on rapid access to trusted biological materials and the infrastructure to produce them at scale,” said Rebecca Bradford, a senior vice president at ATCC. One of the center’s first assignments will be making materials for the National Institutes of Health to use in outbreak research and response.
The center will also develop and test lab models that mimic parts of the human body, including the lungs. ATCC says the models could help researchers evaluate potential treatments while relying less on animal studies. The U.S. Department of Agriculture will also use the center to help advance vaccine and treatment research.
How the expansion came together
Construction began in September 2024, when Virginia announced it had competed with Maryland for the project and approved an $800,000 grant. The state also offered recruitment and training through its Virginia Talent Accelerator Program. ATCC has been based at Innovation Park since 1998 and has research centers in Gaithersburg and Germantown, Maryland.
Federal funding included a construction grant from the National Institutes of Health and a separate grant from the National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases. The latter helped fund the center’s research and pandemic preparedness work.

NHTSA Reports US Traffic Fatalities Dropped 2.5 Percent in H1 2026
26 photos
Photo: IIHS on YouTube
The number of US motor vehicle crash fatalities has reportedly fallen by 2.5 percent in the first six months of 2026, even as American motorists drove 0.8 percent more miles than a year earlier. According to the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration, no fewer than 16,750 deaths were recorded between January and June of this year as opposed to 17,175 during the same period in 2025.
Looking at the raw data more closely, we can see that said 2.5 percent improvement was heavily concentrated in the first quarter. The second delivered almost no year-over-year reduction. Looking at the bigger picture, 425 fewer deaths in the span of six months isn't the flex certain people think it is. Based on these figures, the fatality rate fell to 1.02 deaths per 100 million vehicle miles traveled.
That is the real flex here, representing the second-lowest H1 figure in the agency's historical comparison. During the first half of 2014, the NHTSA reported a record 1.01 deaths per 100 million miles. Between January and March, the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration estimates that 7,715 peeps died in motor vehicle crashes on US roads, a 5 percent decrease from Q1 2025.
The estimated toll reached 9,035 in the second quarter compared with 9,055 a year earlier. When it comes to monthly fatalities, May and June went in the opposite direction of the first four months. NHTSA estimates increases of 1.5 and 3 percent, respectively, compared with last year's corresponding months.
If we analyze the data through monthly breakdowns, the most sensible among us would not treat the decline as a consistently improving trend. The second-quarter numbers suggest that considerable momentum was lost as the year progressed and the weather got warmer. Going down the rabbit hole, state-level data shows something else.
Photo: IIHS on YouTube Per the NHTSA, 35 states and Puerto Rico experienced fewer traffic fatalities during the first half of 2026. If you ask me, I can easily understand Puerto Rico's evolution in this regard after Bad Bunny made everyone love dancing again. Jokes aside, the remaining 15 states and the District of Columbia are projected to have recorded increases.
Hawaii posted the largest decrease among the states, falling 32.4 percent from 68 to 46. West Virginia followed with a 27.8 percent reduction, while Illinois saw its projected fatalities decline 20.4 percent. North Dakota recorded a 25 percent increase, while Delaware and DC increased 28.3 and 128.6 percent. Bear in mind that small underlying numbers can make percentage comparisons sensitive to individual cases.
Texas fatalities remained almost unchanged at 1,851, and California's estimate increased to 1,825 in the analyzed period. Eight of the NHTSA's ten administrative regions are projected to have recorded declines in both fatalities and the fatality rate per 100 million miles, The other two regions are listed with estimated increases of 4 and 3 percent, respectively.
Under the P2SS action plan, the NHTSA will strengthen cooperation with police deps to identify dangerous driving and stop motorists from engaging in risky or illegal behavior. The NHTSA also highlighted increased support for prehospital blood transfusion programs, namely programs allowing medical personnel to administer blood to severely injured crash victims before reaching a hospital.
Research shows that prehospital transfusions may reduce mortality among patients suffering from severe bleeding by 37 percent. While not a 37 percent reduction in overall traffic fatalities, a greater chance of survival among a specific group of seriously injured patients is an improvement all of us can get behind.

Driven: 2026 Subaru Trailseeker (e-Outback) Proves the Boxer Engine Isn't Everything
54 photos
Photo: Florin Profir/autoevolution
Same tune, different song. Known as the Trailseeker in the United States, the Subaru e-Outback is essentially the same electric SUV wearing a different nameplate for European customers. Both versions roll off the same assembly line at Subaru's Gunma Yajima plant in Japan, where production began in February 2026.
The e-Outback also shares its underpinnings with the Toyota bZ4X Touring , another product of the Japanese automakers' long-standing partnership. However, Subaru insists that its electric SUV has received its own engineering tweaks, including suspension tuning, intended to make it more off-road-ready than its Toyota-badged brother. The main question is: is there enough Subaru DNA beneath the skin to back up that claim?
At first glance, the e-Outback bears a clear family resemblance to its combustion-powered namesake. Its rugged proportions, raised stance, and generous plastic cladding suggest that Subaru hasn't forgotten what made the Outback popular in the first place. However, the electric version features a considerably smaller front grille, which makes sense considering that under the hood there is no internal combustion engine.
Above the headlights, the slim LED daytime running lights resemble Spock's raised eyebrows, a distinctive feature of Subaru's latest design language. It's a slightly unusual look, but one that gives the e-Outback, or the 2026 Trailseeker, a recognizable face.
Design evaluation Viewed from the side, the electric crossover looks more like a station wagon on stilts than a conventional SUV. In that respect, it follows the recipe established decades ago with the first-generation Legacy Outback, whose legacy lives on this battery-powered successor. The Forester, meanwhile, has taken the role of the more traditional SUV in Subaru's lineup, after the Tribeca's dismissal.
Photo: Florin Profir/autoevolution The extensive plastic cladding around the wheel arches and lower body panels might initially seem excessive. However, I found myself appreciating those protective elements after an unscheduled encounter with some bushes during the off-road test. The paint emerged unscratched, and even the plastic showed no visible marks from the branches.
In other words, the crossover's rugged aspect isn't just for show. It's not dressed to impress, but to announce that it's ready for your next outdoor adventure.
Interior Assessment Step inside the Subaru e-Outback, and you'll discover an interior that gets quite a few things right, although some of the manufacturer's decisions might leave you scratching your head. For starters, there's no glovebox. Subaru needed that place for some technical components, so it left it without one of the most traditional storage compartments in a car ever.
However, it put a generous storage compartment between the front seats, with a clever dual-opening lid. Rather than being rear-hinged, it opens on either side, allowing both the driver and front passenger to access it comfortably. The compartment is wide but relatively shallow, yet there's more than enough room for your favorite road-trip snacks, with some space left over for essentials.
Photo: Florin Profir/autoevolution There's no head-up display either, not even on the options list. Instead, Subaru placed the digital instrument panel high enough so you won't need an HUD. It's well organized, easy to read, and offers several customization options. You can't arrange everything everywhere, but there's enough flexibility to choose the information that matters most to you.
The center console features two wireless phone chargers, while the transmission controls, drive mode selectors, and camera buttons are positioned behind them, closer to the armrest. Below, the automaker added another open storage area, useful for a purse, some additional snacks, and a few USB charging ports.
Comfort equipment depends on the trim level, as usual. However, the good thing is that all versions are getting the same drivetrain. While the entry-level version comes with fabric upholstery, the top-shelf variant gets heated and cooled front seats, a panoramic glass roof that doesn't open, and a Harman Kardon premium audio system. For the U.S. market, the leather seats are one step above the Touring grade.
Those seated in the back have little to complain about. There's plenty of legroom and headroom. Three adults can sit comfortably. In addition, the seatback offers two reclining positions, allowing passengers to prioritize comfort or free up some additional cargo space, thanks to the 60/40 split-folding mechanism.
Driving take With two electric motors driving all four wheels, the 2026 Subaru Trailseeker (e-Outback) delivers its power smoothly and progressively, as you'd expect from an EV. However, stamp on the skinny pedal and the rear end squats slightly before the vehicle shoots forward like a cannonball. That's so Subaru.
Photo: Florin Profir/autoevolution The automaker claims a 0 to 100 kph (0-62 mph) run in 4.4 seconds, making the e-Outback the quickest in the model in Subaru's current lineup by that measure. However, using a GPS-based smartphone app, we recorded times below four seconds with the battery charged above 80 percent. There was a catch, though. In our case, after two consecutive launches, the car became more relaxed, suggesting that its electronics were limiting performance to protect the powertrain.
Despite its impressive straight-line performance, the e-Outback isn't particularly interested in pretending to be a sports car. The steering feels somewhat numb, while the soft suspension allows noticeable body roll around corners. Interestingly, the vehicle maintains its composure and grips remarkably well, but the body movements discourage enthusiastic driving long before the chassis approaches its actual limits.
On the other hand, the same suspension setup makes the Trailseeker a remarkably smooth companion on uneven roads. Rather than chasing sharp handling, Subaru appears to prioritize ride quality and comfort, a decision that makes perfect sense considering the vehicle's intended purpose as a family car.
Fortunately, the braking system is more reassuring. The transition between the regenerative braking and conventional friction brakes is exceptionally smooth, with no perceptible change in pedal feel. In addition, the paddles behind the steering wheel let you adjust how aggressive the regenerative braking can be, although one-pedal-drive is not present.
Photo: Florin Profir/autoevolution However, the biggest surprise comes when you leave the pavement behind. Despite riding on 20-inch wheels wrapped in Dunlop Sport Maxx tires, the e-Outback exceeded my expectations on a damp off-road course featuring steep climbs, descents, slide slopes, and plenty of mud.
Much of the credit goes to Subaru's X-MODE system, which manages traction and allows different degrees of wheelspin, depending on the selected setting. Whether climbing steep ramps covered in wet grass or negotiating muddy sections, the system continuously adjusted the available traction. I deliberately pushed the e-Outback into situations where grip was scarce, trying to find its limits. Yet, the electronics repeatedly stepped in to manage power delivery and save the day.
From behind the wheel, it's really tempting to believe that you're demonstrating some impressive off-road driving skills. In reality, electronics are doing much of the heavy lifting, helping you escape situations your own overconfidence might have gotten you into.
On one particular, grass-covered slope, the hill-descent function proved its ability to keep the car in a straight line. I didn't have to touch any pedals. No drama, no fuss, just the electronics quietly doing their job.
Photo: Florin Profir/autoevolution The 8.5-inch ground clearance, short front overhang, and underbody protection further inspire confidence when tackling uneven terrain. Combined with the capable all-wheel-drive system, these features make the e-Outback (Trailseeker) a convincing choice for weekend adventurers, rather than another electric crossover that merely looks the part and struggles climbing a curb at the mall.
Everyday Living If the Outback's soft suspension and somewhat numb steering discourage spirited driving, they become welcome companions during the daily commute. The ride is great, the seats provide excellent support, and the cabin remains quiet, with little noticeable tire or wind noise. Generous side windows and the available panoramic glass roof, which has a retractable shade but cannot be opened, further enhance the sense of space.
Subaru also paid attention to some minor practical details. The doors extend over the lower sills, protecting them from mud and road grime. After our off-road adventure, I was particularly grateful for this arrangement. Otherwise, I might still be cleaning mud off my pants, shoes, and upholstery. It's not a first in the industry, but there are many other SUV-manufacturers that don't make this.
The cargo area is spacious and regularly shaped, although the loading lip is higher than on a conventional station wagon. Considering the vehicle's generous ground clearance, that's a reasonable compromise. Besides, taller drivers might appreciate not having to bend quite so far when retrieving luggage.
Photo: Florin Profir/autoevolution For the onboard infotainment system, the car proved effective. It seamlessly paired wirelessly with Android Auto and Apple CarPlay devices, while the built-in navigation system offers another useful feature. Enter a charging station as your destination, and the vehicle automatically starts battery preconditioning to prepare it for DC charging. Ideally, the station should be at least 30 minutes away, depending on the outside temperature.
During our test, we observed a charging power of 113 kW just a few minutes after plugging in, with an estimated time of approximately 30 minutes to reach 80 percent. When we returned 40 minutes later, the battery was sitting comfortably at the 80% charging limit, for another adventure. We had deliberately selected that limit to help preserve battery longevity.
Energy consumption ranged between 20 and 24 kWh/100 km (2.6-3.1 miles/kWh), depending on the driving conditions and how enthusiastically we used the accelerator. With the battery at 80 percent, the instrument cluster estimated about 170 miles (274 km) of remaining range, suggesting a real-world range of about 200 miles (320 km) on a full charge. Considering that ambient temperatures ranged between 39 and 63 degrees Fahrenheit (4-17 Celsius), that's a respectable result for an all-wheel-drive electric SUV riding on 20-inch wheels.
The 20-inch wheels fitted on our test vehicle also come with an efficiency penalty compared with the available 18-inch alternatives. If maximizing range is your priority, the smaller ones would be the better choice.
Photo: Florin Profir/autoevolution Subaru could probably have squeezed a few more miles out of the 74.2 kWh battery with a more aerodynamically optimized body. Instead, it chose to build something that actually looks like a Subaru, rather than another anonYmous electric crossover shaped primarily by the demands of the wind tunnel and the accountants.
Test Drive Round-up There's plenty of Subaru DNA included in the e-Outback, or the Trailseeker, bodywork, and I'm not talking about its vivid blue paint. The way it reminded me of a second-generation Forester, particularly when the pavement disappeared and the going got tough. There's no flat-four engine under the hood, no conventional driveshaft connecting the axles, and no mechanical center differential distributing torque.
Yet, the way the electric all-wheel-drive system manages traction feels remarkably familiar to anyone who has spent time behind the wheel of a traditional Subaru.
The e-Outback does everything you'd expect from an adventurous crossover, and then some. It also proves that electrification doesn't necessarily mean abandoning the qualities that made a brand successful in the first place.
Photo: Florin Profir/autoevolution There's even a little luxury for those who enjoy getting away from civilization without giving up every creature comfort. With the available vehicle-to-load capability, you could take an espresso machine into the wilderness and enjoy a proper morning coffee surrounded by nature. Just remember to plan your charging stops and keep an eye on the remaining range.
As for the pricing, we're using the American Trailseeker as our reference, since it's the U.S.-market counterpart of the e-Outback tested here. The Trailseeker starts at $39,995 for the Premium. The Limited starts at $43,995 and ads a 120-volt power outlet in the cargo area, while the better-equipped Touring costs $46,555. The Touring Leather ads another $300.
These are manufacturer-suggested retail prices , excluding destination charges, sales taxes, and registration fees. Our e-Outback tested was about the same price as its American sibling, at roughly EUR 50,000.
Yes, we know there are many other electric SUVs on the market that are worth considering. Some of them may offer better efficiency or sharper handling. But if you're looking for the same peace of mind you've come to expect from Subaru, or from a dependable Toyota, there's little reason to change a winning recipe simply because automotive fashion has moved on.
Photo: Florin Profir/autoevolution
The e-Outback, like its Trailseeker twin brother, isn't perfect. Its steering could use more feedback, its energy consumption is not the best in class, and the missing glovebox remains a peculiar decision. But it's comfortable, generously equipped, surprisingly capable off-road, and unmistakably Subaru where it matters most.
The boxer engine may be gone, but the adventurous spirit is alive and kickin'.

Rates, capacity, earnings and the supply chain risks shaping air cargo into 2027
A review of 2026 air cargo demand, rates and capacity, carrier and forwarder earnings, and how much slack the system has left, using SONAR data.
EXECUTIVE SUMMARY Air cargo entered 2026 expecting lower rates and got rates roughly 30% higher instead. The February escalation of the Middle East conflict removed about 12% of global capacity overnight, jet fuel doubled, and AI hardware filled the planes that were left. The result is a market running with almost no slack, where a single disruption can halt flows with little warning, as the Nov. 13 FAA ground stop showed. Key findings: SONAR’s Freightos Air Index (FAX.GLBL) averaged $3.11/kg in October, up 36% year over year, and $3.44/kg in November to date (+39%). U.S. outbound scheduled capacity (OACT.USA) ran about 4% to 8% below 2025 for nine straight months before turning positive in October, led by freighters (OACTF.USA, +11% to +14%) rather than passenger bellies. Forwarders with AI and data center exposure posted sharp air profit gains, winning on rate more than volume. Ocean volumes to the U.S. are still growing, so air’s gains came from high-value freight rather than a broad shift off the water. The risks heading into 2027 are fragility, fuel and demand concentration, not a lack of freight.

Ivana Rubino has joined neurodegenerative biotech ProMIS Neurosciences as chief commercial officer, with 15 years of experience in the brutal Alzheimer’s field as her guide.
ProMIS Neurosciences’ new Chief Commercial Officer Ivana Rubino has been in the room for some of the proudest and most heartbreaking moments in Alzheimer’s disease drug development over the past 15 years—first at Roche, then at Biogen.
She never expected to be there.
“I come from a little, little town in Sicily, and never in my life I would have thought that I would have been part of so many historical moment in Alzheimer disease,” Rubino told BioSpace .
But this disease space, as challenging as it is, has become her life’s work. Rubino joined ProMIS , a biotech developing therapeutic antibodies and vaccines to target misfolded proteins for neurodegenerative diseases, in October as CCO. She arrived there from Biogen, after spending more than six years working on Leqembi.
Rubino felt losses like Roche’s gantenerumab, which was discontinued in 2022 , and the debacle around Biogen’s Aduhelm personally.
“We have gone through a lot of negative experience and negative trials, and I know in the moment they felt terrible,” Rubino said. “Your personal life and your professional life tend to really blend.”
Alzheimer’s disease

But Rubino’s drive to do more to help patients with neurodegenerative disease has never dimmed, and that’s what brought her to ProMIS.
“Now I am in a better place to reflect back. We learn so much,” she said. “I know it feels almost cheesy. We all say, ‘Oh, from a failure you learn,’ but in Alzheimer’s, it’s so true because each trial built upon the learning from the previous one.”
From gantenerumab—which failed in two Phase 3 studies in November 2022—the industry learned to select patients based on the presence of amyloid in the brain. With Aduhelm, which was approved as the first anti-amyloid antibody in 2021 but then pulled from the market a few years later, PET scans were introduced. This in turn brought awareness of amyloid-related imaging abnormalities (ARIA), a side effect of the next anti-amyloid antibodies to receive approval, Leqembi and Eli Lilly’s Kisunla. Rubino said researchers realized better ways to manage the side effects and titration with that discovery.
“We always knew that the first approval would have been the first and not the last, and from there we can build the next chapter,” Rubino said.
ProMIS looks to the future
ProMIS is doing just that, with PMN310 in Phase 1b testing for Alzheimer’s. The drug still goes after amyloid, like Leqembi and Kisunla, but builds on the understanding from those therapies to more selectively engage the toxic oligomers of amyloid beta.
“That’s really under the premise that plaque removal may be highly associated with ARIA,” Rubino explained. “What if we were not to target directly the plaques, but going almost through a backdoor targeting the oligomers?”
Other therapies in earlier development at ProMIS include a vaccine to prevent Alzheimer’s, plus programs for ALS, Parkinson’s disease and other types of dementia.
Alzheimer’s disease

After covering the Alzheimer’s space through every high and low, BioSpace ’s Annalee Armstrong welcomes back Roche for the 2026 Alzheimer’s Renaissance.

From her experience at Biogen, Rubino took some hard lessons. After Aduhelm was ultimately pulled from the market in 2024, her team had a lot of work to do to re-establish trust. In addition, because the availability of monoclonal antibodies for Alzheimer’s was a practice-changing event for doctors, Biogen’s commercial teams had to start from scratch with education.
“Usually we think about a drug as something that alleviates our symptoms and makes you feel better, but these drugs have a different profile,” Rubino explained. “They delay the decline in the disease, which is a much tougher conversation to have with patients.”
The Alzheimer’s space requires a strong connection between industry, clinicians, advocacy groups and patients, Rubino added.
With that lesson in mind, Rubino was brought on to ProMIS to create a commercial strategy even though PMN310 is only in early-stage clinical trials. A key readout is expected from the Phase 1b 144-patient PRECISE-AD study in 2027, at which point Rubino will start to think about how PMN310 might be used in the real world. That means designing a precise Phase 3 trial that will aid critical conversation with providers later on.
“The Phase 3 will always be your best experiment for a drug,” Rubino said. “Whatever you do in the post-marketing setting will never have that level of precision of a Phase 3.”
An interim analysis of the Phase 1b trial for PMN310 in July showed very low rates of ARIA, comparable with background rates in the average population, Rubino noted.
This early readout helped Rubino make the decision to jump from the larger-cap pharma world to ProMIS. The results were encouraging—but Rubino is cautious, because she knows all too well how quickly things can change after a long clinical trial in Alzheimer’s.
“Alzheimer’s is not for the faint of heart, but when you get to the finish line, the feeling is incredible because you really feel you are advancing medical history,” she said.

RELEX Solutions has acquired autone, a London-based company that helps fashion, sports, and lifestyle brands plan their inventory. It's RELEX's seventh acquisition.
What’s Related
Autone will become the core of a new business unit called RELEX Lifestyle, focused on fashion, sports and lifestyle retail . Alex Chataigner will lead the new unit.
Founded in 2021, autone helps brands make better buying, allocation, and replenishment decisions over the course of a season. Its team includes former merchandisers, inventory planners, and data scientists who worked at fashion and luxury brands. Customers include Roberto Cavalli, Cult Gaia, Vilebrequin, Lancel, IKKS, and the jewelry division of Galeries Lafayette. The Kooples recently picked autone for buying and allocation on its seasonal collections, and British luxury brand Sunspel is using it to automate replenishment and rebalancing across its stores worldwide.
RELATED: Supply Chain Leaders Give Their AI Readiness a 4.9 Out of 10 Score
The challenge of planning in fashion
Fashion is hard to plan. New collections often have no sales history, buying decisions happen months before products reach stores, and the window to sell at full price can be short.
Autone forecasts demand using product attributes and how similar items sold in past collections. It predicts demand down to the product, store, size, and color. That helps teams buy smarter before a season starts and move inventory around as demand shifts.
One French luxury leather goods brand cut its rebalancing time by 90%, from two and a half days to two hours, and reported a 10% revenue increase.
“We founded autone because we lived it firsthand. Before autone, we did this job inside luxury houses: the endless firefighting, collections overproduced and heading for markdowns, shortages that left stores empty, and brilliant teams patching a broken system with spreadsheets. So we built the tool we wished we had,” said Adil Bouhdadi, CEO of autone.
One system for many products
RELEX says the deal gives fashion retailers one engine for both seasonal and continuous ranges, with one interface and one partner . That covers everything from financial and assortment planning through markdowns, clearance, rebalancing, and buying.
“Fashion retail has unique planning challenges that require a deep understanding of how the industry operates,” said Mikko Kärkkäinen, Group CEO and co-founder of RELEX Solutions. “The autone team brings that expertise, along with technology developed specifically for the decisions fashion retailers make every day.”
Intersport France already uses RELEX to pull its planning into one system, and it sees autone as a good addition. “The fashion and sports expertise from autone complements this approach, helping our retailers buy closer to real demand throughout the season,” said Gérard Leclerc, President, Belgium, Spain and Portugal, Intersport France.

Ford Bronco Dahaidao Edition Debuts in China, So This Is What We're Missing
7 photos
Photo: Ford
Ford unveiled the all-new Bronco Dahaidao Edition in China, and it looks like it could fit right in in the United States. The new off-road-focused variant is scheduled to make public debut at the Guangzhou Auto Show later this week with Bronco Heritage Edition-like looks and 35-inch off-road tires.
The all-new Ford Bronco Dahiadao Edition is inspired by the Bronco' s racing heritage at the Baja 1000 and named after China’s uninhabited Dahaidao Gobi desert crossing in Xinjiang. The model is finished in vibrant red and features a removable white hardtop, contrasting black wheel arches, and large white "BRONCO" decals so onlookers know what they're dealing with.
The off-roader rides on two-tone silver and black beadlock-capable wheels with all-terrain tires. It sports front and rear differentials, stands at 10.75 inches (273 millimeters) of ground clearance on FOX 2.5-inch shock absorbers, and has a wading depth of 33.4 inches (850 millimeters), backed by underbody steel skid plates and high-clearance fenders, all confirming its off-road abilities.
Built on a body-on-frame chassis and sitting on the Ford T6 platform, just like its American sibling, the special edition is offered exclusively as a four-door. Those doors open to a cabin that is different from what we all know from the U.S.-spec Bronco .
Photo: Ford China Unlike the model selling in America, the Chinese Broncos run an upgraded system powered by a Qualcomm Snapdragon 8155 chip on a 12.3-inch digital instrument cluster and a 12-inch central touchscreen.
The Chinese Bronco retains physical rubberized buttons and toggle switches on the center console for the locking diffs and 4WD modes, plus the overhead auxiliary switches pre-wired for aftermarket lights or winches. Rugged, easy-to-clean upholstery, a Bang & Olufsen sound system, and PVC washout flooring with drain plugs are also on the menu in typical off-road fashion.
Under the hood of the Dahaidao Edition sits the 2.3-liter EcoBoost turbocharged inline-four, the only option available in China. The inline-four produces 271 horsepower (275 metric horsepower) and 316 pound-feet (429 Newton meters) of torque. A ten-speed automatic transmission puts the power down through all four corners.
The all-new Bronco Dahaidao Edition will roll off the production line of the Jiangling-Ford joint venture starting this winter. Ford has no plans to bring it to North America, where the closest visual and mechanical equivalents are the Bronco Heritage Edition when it comes to the red-and-white retro appearance, and the Sasquatch Package, which also rides on 35-inch tires.
Photo: Ford China The automaker hasn’t disclosed pricing details yet, but it will probably do so during the Guangzhou Auto Show later this week. The all-new Ford Bronco Dahaidao Edition is expected to start at around 299,800 yuan, which translates to roughly $41,500. In the U.S., the similar Bronco Heritage Edition is a $52,620 deal.

Niron Magnetics will build a $1.8 billion manufacturing campus in Dothan, Alabama, to make rare-earth-free permanent magnets at high volume. Gov. Kay Ivey announced the project on Nov. 20.
What’s Related
The 1.6-million-square-foot campus will go on the Westgate Super Site, a 446-acre industrial park in Houston County. The plant is designed to make 10,000 tons of magnets a year and is expected to create about 700 high-wage jobs within five years. Construction is set to start in 2028, and production should begin in 2029.
Niron is a Minneapolis company founded in 2013. It makes Iron Nitride magnets from abundant domestic materials and pitches them as a lower-cost alternative to neodymium magnets, which rely on rare earths. Its magnets go into AI infrastructure , cars, industrial equipment, and consumer electronics .
“Alabama has demonstrated time and time again that when it comes to competing for the world's most transformative industries, we are second to none,” Ivey said.
Why Dothan won out
Niron looked at a lot of options before it landed in the Wiregrass.
“Every step of the way, Alabama treated our success as its own,” said Niron CEO Jonathan Rowntree. “We considered sites in 22 states, and Alabama stood out from the very first conversation.”
The site was ready for a project like this. The City of Dothan, Houston County, the city's Industrial Development Board, and the Dothan Area Chamber of Commerce spent several years developing it. It got funding from the state's SEEDS site program in 2024 and later from the Growing Alabama Tax Credit program. The park also has a CSX rail line and earned CSX Select Site Platinum status in late 2025. Real estate firm Savills advised Niron on the search.
A much bigger second plant
Dothan will be home to Niron's second high-volume plant. The first one, in Sartell, Minnesota, opens in 2027 and can make up to 1,500 tons of magnets a year. The Alabama plant is designed to make more than six times that amount.
According to the state, about 90% of global rare-earth magnet production happens overseas. Officials say the Dothan plant will help build up U.S. supply chains for automotive , advanced technology , and defense.
Dothan Mayor Mark Saliba said the payoff for local families is the big story.
“This project means opportunity,” Saliba said. “It means families can build their futures here with state-of-the-art technology that will strengthen America's supply chain and our national security , which our country depends on.”

Alia CTOL Flight Seals BETA’s Partnership with Sinclair Community College
8 photos
Photo: Sinclair Community College
BETA is, without a doubt, one of the most successful electric aircraft maker in the global market right now, and one of its most recent partnership proves that this success extends beyond commercial and defense applications, to the academic environment as well. It’s not just about making eVTOLs, but also teaching the next generations how to better integrate them.
This has been a very busy and life-changing year for Beta Technologies, with its CTOL (the conventional takeoff and landing version of its flagship electric aircraft) landing at the center of historic aviation operations in New Zealand, the UK, and back home in the US, through its dazzling participation in the eIPP
.
After all of these milestones, the Alia CTOL nailed one more, with a demonstration flight at the National Advanced Air Mobility Center of Excellence (NAAMCE), located at Springfield-Beckley Municipal Airport. The pilot was Kyle Clark himself, BETA founder and chief executive officer, and his passenger was Sinclair President and CEO Dr. Steven Johnson.
The flight demonstration came as the perfect way to seal a pioneering partnership for AAM (Advanced Air Mobility) and the world of academia. Sinclair Community College was the first academic institution of any kind in the US to purchase a BETA flight simulator, and will soon be the first to actually own an Alia electric aircraft.
This is all part of developing a complex training program that will give students first-hand access to an actual electric aircraft and the technical skills required to build a career in electric aviation. With eVTOLs and other types of electric aircraft closer to commercial service, there’s an obvious need for supporting training programs in higher education.
A new generation of pilots, technicians, and maintenance personnel, is part of this new era of air mobility, and Sinclair is ready to be one of the first to support it, especially given Ohio’s strong aviation background, confirmed through the recent publication of an Advanced Air Mobility (AAM) Action Plan by the Ohio Department of Transportation (ODOT).
BETA is not only the name behind the Alia eVTOL and CTOL, but also the only manufacturer in this industry that has also developed a certified electric aircraft charging system. With more than 160 multimodal charging sites currently active, BETA has an impressive electric charging network that keeps growing. These exact charging capabilities were also installed at NAAMCE in Springfield, in preparation for this demonstration flight and future flights.
The Alia CTOL has recently wrapped up its spectacular participation in the eIPP (it was selected to participate in seven of the total of eight programs), with Florida as the final state, where it has completed 14 flights, covering close to 700 nautical miles. Alia CTOL has also been selected by New Zealand’s Air New Zealand and Loganair in the UK for pioneering electric aviation operations.

ASUS Turbo Radeon AI Pro R9700-Top 3
While much of the attention in the market for AI inference has been focused on servers and datacenter-scale deployments, the heart and soul of the modern AI revolution started with video cards. And that is where it still beats on today, overshadowed by servers but still an important market segment overall.
Within the AMD ecosystem, the company has taken a very visible pivot in how it markets and categorizes its professional video cards. The Radeon Pro lineup, once the backbone of AMD’s workstation graphics efforts, has become the Radeon AI Pro lineup, and the backbone of AMD’s add-in video card/AI accelerator efforts. The flagship for this line, in turn, is the Radeon AI Pro R9700, a 32GB VRAM card that AMD and its partners are positioning as a more budget-friendly alternative to NVIDIA’s RTX PRO Blackwell lineup of workstation cards.
Today we are taking a look at one of those R9700 cards in the form of ASUS’s Turbo Radeon AI Pro R9700. The sub-$2000 card have been heavily optimized for workstation use, balancing graphics needs and display outputs with the ability to fit up to four cards into a single system for larger AI workloads.
ASUS Turbo Radeon AI PRO R9700 Hardware Overview
As AMD is not selling their own reference design workstation cards for this generation, it falls to AMD’s partners to sell the cards instead. Which is a production strategy that they are well-accustomed to on the consumer side of matters, but is a bit more unusual for a workstation card.
Notably, AMD has been keeping their Radeon Pro partners on a rather short leash with card designs. AMD is curating a very specific image for a very specific market here, not the least of which is the ability to install multiple cards in a single workstation. As a result, though AMD is not selling their reference card their partner cards are all quite similar in their high-level design as dual slot blowers, a form factor you will not readily find outside of workstation video cards these days.
That brings us to ASUS’s Turbo Radeon AI PRO R9700. ASUS has long been a heavyweight in the world of video cards, so it is no surprise to see them jump on board producing a Radeon Pro card.
ASUS Turbo Radeon AI Pro R9700-Top Angled 1
ASUS’s R9700 card is, in all practical application, exactly what you would expect from a workstation card given the form factor and the AMD’s constraints. This is a dual slot video card that follows the PCIe specifications to a T in terms of width and height, in order to ensure that it (and perhaps a few of its friends) can fit into a workstation chassis.
ASUS Turbo Radeon AI R9700 Specifications
CUs | 64
AI Accelerators | 128
GPU Boost Clockspeed | 2.92GHz
Peak Matrix Throughput (FP8) | 382.7 TFLOPS
Peak Vector Throughput (FP32) | 47.8 TFLOPS
Memory | 32GB GDDR6
Memory Bandwidth | 640GB/sec (20Gbps x 256-bits)
ECC | Yes (Linux Only)
Infinity Cache | 64MB
I/O | PCIe Gen5 x16
TBP | 300W
Form Factor | PCIe CEM (Air Cooled)
Dimensions | 267 x 111 x 40 mm (10.5 x 4.4 x 1.6 in)
Architecture | RDNA 4
GPU | Navi 48
Under the hood, the card is powered by AMD’s Navi 48 GPU, which is the most powerful RDNA 4 GPU offered in this generation. The GPU offers 64 of AMD’s CUs, which in turn is comprised of a total of 4096 shading units for vector math and 128 AI accelerator cores for matrix operations.
With a peak clock speed of 2.92GHz, this gives the R9700 a peak matrix math throughput of 382.7 TFLOPS with dense FP8 math, or double that with sparsity. One of the key improvements in this generation of RDNA architecture is the addition of FP8 support, which not only further improves the compute throughput of the card, but it better aligns AMD’s hardware with the general trends in the industry towards lower precision weights, and fitting a large number of weights within a given amount of memory.
On that note, as is traditional for a workstation card, AMD and ASUS have packed the R9700 with as much memory as the card can handle. With Navi 48 sporting a 256-bit bus, the card has been equipped with 32GB of GDDR6 memory organized as 16 2Gbit chips in clamshell mode. Above all else, memory support is a key differentiator between AMD’s consumer and professional cards, so 32GB is something you will only find on the Radeon AI Pro cards.
The GDDR6 memory itself is clocked at 20Gbps, allowing for a total of 640GB/second of memory bandwidth for the card. Soft ECC is also available, though only under Linux (and even then, it has to be manually enabled). This allows for an extra degree of reliability for systems and racks based around the card.
AMD-Navi-48-Die-Shot
Navi 48 itself is somewhere between a mid to high-end GPU as far as die size (357mm2) and transistor counts (53.9B) go, which makes it a bit of an oddity within AMD’s lineup as far as card progression is concerned. AMD did not produce a true high-end GPU this generation, and as a result the R9700 actually has less VRAM than the previous-generation 48GB Radeon Pro W7900. This means that it is a step back in terms of overall memory capacity, but AMD is looking to make up the difference with compute throughput, thanks in large part to the newer chip architecture.
One advantage of being a smaller chip, however, is that it keeps TDPs in check. AMD (and ASUS’s) Total Board Power figure for the card is just 300 Watts, which makes it relatively easy to keep a blower-style card cooled without a blowout on noise. This also means that even 4 cards in a system is not going to result in excessive power requirements, though it will certainly be pushing the limits of a single power supply.
ASUS Turbo Radeon AI PRO R9700 Build and Design
As far as video card designs go, ASUS’s Turbo Radeon AI Pro R9700 is a very typical dual slot blower design. With a need to ensure that the card can be installed in multiples together, ASUS has kept things tightly tuned to PCIe specifications, with a dual slot card measuring 10.5 inches long and 4.4 inches high.
ASUS Turbo Radeon AI Pro R9700-With Box 1
Interestingly, the blower design here is open-backed, that is, the back side of the card has open vents so that the card can pull in air from both sides of the card.
ASUS Turbo Radeon AI Pro R9700-Fan 1
The fan itself is a pretty typical blower design. According to ASUS they are using dual ball bearings here.
ASUS Turbo Radeon AI Pro R9700-Backplate 1
Taking a look at the rear of the card, we can better see the venting cut into the card’s PCB and its shroud. For that matter, we can also see that the card even has a shroud on its back side. As noted earlier, the 32GB of GDDR6 is organized in a clamshell configuration on the R9700, meaning that 8 chips are on the rear of the card and need to be protected and cooled, just as with all of the chips on the front side of the card.
ASUS Turbo Radeon AI Pro R9700-Rear 2
Being that this is a workstation card, ASUS has also put some thought into their power connector placement. The Turbo R9700 uses an ATX 12V-2×6 connector, which has been placed on the rear of the card instead of the top, another workstation-centric design element that makes it easier to install multiple cards in a system. The 12V-2×6 connector is rated for up to 600W, so the 300W TBP R9700 is well within the cable’s limits.
ASUS Turbo Radeon AI Pro R9700-Front Angled 3
Meanwhile, at the front of the card we find a not too subtle reminder that this is a video card, with 4 display outputs – the maximum number of displays the Navi 48 GPU can drive. ASUS has given their card a triple DisplayPort plus single HDMI port configuration. The DisplayPorts are all DisplayPort 2.1a, while the HDMI port supports HDMI 2.1b. Coupled with DSC, and the card can drive displays at up to 12K in resolution.
ASUS Turbo Radeon AI Pro R9700-Front Angled 5
Otherwise, besides the display outputs, the rest of the front of the card is almost entirely vent cut-outs. 300W is still a lot of heat to expel from a blower card, so ASUS does not hold back here, and you can clearly see the fins from the heatsink running within the card.

Of course there’s a catch, because this thing did not start life in this configuration, as it was a 2017 Mercedes-Benz G 550 4x4 Squared when it first came out, and it has Esteem Customs to thank four the 6x6 conversion.
Thus, the third Mercedes-Benz portal axle, as well as the 22-inch Vossen wheels shod in 37-inch M/T tires, the KW racing coilovers, upgraded brakes, and the custom extended chassis and rear bed bodywork have come from the aftermarket realm.
The same goes for the Brabus-style front grille and carbon fiber dual snorkels, as well as the hood, fender covers, flares, door mirror casings, and trim molding, all of which have been made of carbon fiber. The front and rear skid plates, the metal rear bumper guard, power running boards, and exhaust system are other modifications mentioned in the listing. The head unit, Brabus-style blue interior, and floor mats round off the makeover.
Power is supplied by a V8 engine, which is said to have a 4.0-liter displacement. The mill is twin turbocharged, and according to the listing, develops 416 hp (422 ps/310 kW) and 450 pound-feet (610 Nm) of torque. Everything is channeled to all six wheels through a seven-speed automatic transmission, and a two-speed transfer case. The ad also mentions the independent differential locks, and the portal axles for enhanced off-roading prowess.
Photo: Cars&Bids This older Mercedes-Benz G 550 4x4 Squared that has become a veritable 6x6 is presented in Designo Manufaktur Sintered Bronze Magno, on top of a blue interior. It features a Harman Kardon sound system, Apple CarPlay and Android Auto compatibility, Bluetooth connectivity, and other stuff that is mentioned in the ad.
Care to talk about the known flaws? Well, a TPMS (tire pressure monitoring system) light is illuminated. And that’s not all, because the Carfax report reveals that this six-wheel drive beast sustained “minor” damage to the front end as a result of a collision with a vehicle recorded at the end of 2024. However, the airbags did not deploy during the accident.
The six-wheel drive Mercedes G-Wagen in question is said to have had all portal axles serviced, as well as all differentials, and the rear transfer case. The rear driveshafts were replaced and balanced, and the engine oil and filter were changed, the selling dealer reported.
According to the ad, the vendor bought this G-Class earlier in 2026, adding some 2,000 miles (3,200 km) since. The vehicle had around 8,000 miles (12,800 km) on the clock at the time of cataloging. It is accompanied by the paint-matched fiberglass fender flares, and one key, and you can find it on Cars&Bids here , as part of an online auction that will end on November 30, 2026. The highest bid was $105,000 at the time of writing. How much is this ride worth to you?

source_document.body:
For decades, electric utilities have planned around a relatively predictable relationship between population growth, economic activity, weather and electricity consumption. Demand increased gradually, infrastructure investments followed long-term forecasts and utilities generally had time to prepare for changes in where and how electricity was consumed.
That planning model is being tested. The U.S. Energy Information Administration (EIA) projected that commercial electricity sales would surpass residential sales in 2026, as overall U.S. electricity consumption reaches new highs. The rapid expansion of artificial intelligence (AI) data centers, growth in other large commercial facilities and continued electrification are reshaping the electricity landscape.
COMMENTARY
But the significance of this crossover extends well beyond which customer class consumes the most electricity. It signals a fundamental change in the scale, location and concentration of demand, one that challenges the assumptions utilities have relied on for decades.
A single large commercial customer can introduce hundreds of megawatts of new demand into a relatively small geographic area, sometimes on timelines that outpace the planning, permitting and construction of traditional grid infrastructure. At the same time, distributed energy resources (DERs), electric vehicles (EVs) and behind-the-meter technologies are making electricity flows increasingly dynamic.
The question is no longer simply how many additional megawatts the grid will need. Utilities must also understand where those megawatts are needed, when demand will materialize and how much capacity can be made available through better use of existing infrastructure.
Not All Grid Capacity is Created Equal
One of the biggest challenges with commercial-led load growth is that available grid capacity is not evenly distributed. A utility may have sufficient generation resources or capacity across its broader service territory while facing significant constraints at the substations, feeders or transmission facilities serving a proposed commercial development. In other words, having enough electricity available in aggregate does not necessarily mean it can be delivered where a customer needs it.
Consider the scale of emerging AI infrastructure. Projects such as the Stargate-associated Crusoe data center campus in Abilene, Texas, illustrate the magnitude of the challenge, with development plans at approximately 1 GW. At that scale, accommodating new demand becomes a major transmission, generation and regional infrastructure planning consideration. While projects of this magnitude create significant transmission and regional planning challenges, the same fundamental questions about location, timing and available capacity also apply at the distribution level, where much smaller loads can create highly localized constraints.
But utilities do not need a gigawatt-scale project to encounter serious capacity constraints. Consider a commercial facility proposing to add 20 MWs of demand within an existing distribution service area. Whether the utility can accommodate that load depends on the configuration and capacity of the surrounding network, including feeder and substation capabilities, transformer loading, voltage conditions, existing customer demand and the facility’s operating profile.
A feeder that appears to have available capacity during much of the year may approach its operating limits during a handful of summer afternoons. Another feeder may have more consistent headroom but require significant upgrades to support the customer’s full requested load. These distinctions matter because the infrastructure required to resolve each situation could be very different.
The first scenario might benefit from targeted load management or flexibility during constrained periods. The second may require physical upgrades regardless of how effectively existing resources are managed. Utilities must therefore move beyond simply estimating aggregate demand growth and toward understanding where and when new loads intersect with actual system constraints.
From Static Forecasting to Locational Grid Intelligence
Traditional load forecasting remains essential to utility planning. Long-term projections guide investments in generation, transmission, substations and other infrastructure that can take years to develop. However, the emerging load environment requires utilities to connect those long-range forecasts with a more granular understanding of distribution-system conditions.
Advanced metering infrastructure (AMI), grid-edge sensors, distribution automation systems and other operational technologies can provide utilities with a more detailed understanding of conditions across the distribution network. When combined with network models and analytics, these data sources can help utilities evaluate transformer and feeder loading, voltage conditions, localized demand peaks and the effects of distributed energy resources.
This information becomes particularly valuable when utilities connect it with advanced analytics and more dynamic forecasting models. Return to the example of a proposed 20 MW commercial load. A conventional planning approach might evaluate the customer’s requested peak demand against the capacity of the surrounding system. A more adaptive approach would examine how that demand is expected to develop and interact with existing grid conditions.
Will the facility require the full 20 MW immediately, or will its demand increase over several years? Will its peak coincide with the system’s existing summer peak? Are nearby customers adding EV charging, rooftop solar or battery storage? How will those resources affect the local load profile? Most importantly, is the resulting constraint persistent, or does it occur only during a limited number of high-stress hours?
These questions can produce very different investment decisions. For example, a feeder that exceeds its operating threshold for a few hours each year presents a different planning problem than one that is consistently overloaded. Both conditions require attention, but they do not necessarily require the same solution. More granular forecasting can help utilities distinguish between those situations, evaluate potential scenarios and identify where infrastructure investments will deliver the greatest benefit.
This is where grid-edge intelligence becomes especially important. Rather than relying exclusively on historical averages or system-level assumptions, utilities can use more detailed operational information to understand how their infrastructure is performing under actual conditions. That visibility does not create physical capacity on its own. It does, however, provide a stronger foundation for determining where additional investment is genuinely necessary.
Flexibility Becomes Part of the Capacity Equation
Once utilities understand where and when capacity constraints are likely to occur, another opportunity emerges: determining whether some portion of those constraints can be addressed using flexible resources already connected to the grid.
For years, demand response programs largely focused on reducing systemwide peak demand. Today, the growing number of distributed resources creates opportunities to apply flexibility more precisely, matching available resources with specific local grid needs. Residential batteries, smart thermostats, EV chargers, electric water heaters, distributed generation and controllable commercial loads can potentially reduce, shift or otherwise manage demand during constrained periods.
Consider a distribution feeder that experiences capacity limitations during several late-afternoon hours in August. If a utility can reliably coordinate nearby batteries, EV charging and other controllable loads during those periods, it may be able to reduce stress on the feeder without immediately rebuilding every affected asset.
That does not mean flexibility can replace traditional infrastructure. It cannot resolve every thermal limitation, voltage problem or reliability requirement, and a persistent capacity shortage will often demand physical upgrades.
But when the constraint is temporary, flexibility can become a valuable operational tool. The challenge is making that flexibility dependable enough to factor into planning and operational decisions. Five megawatts of enrolled flexible capacity sounds promising. But that number has limited value if the resources are not located behind the relevant constraint, cannot respond during the required hours or cannot sustain their response long enough to address the problem.
Utilities need to know not just how much flexibility exists, but how quickly it can respond and whether it performs as expected. This is where distributed energy resource management systems (DERMS) are becoming increasingly important. By coordinating distributed resources across customer programs and grid operations, DERMS can help utilities identify available flexibility, dispatch resources against specific system needs and measure their performance.
The distinction is important. A resource that participates in a broad demand response program may help reduce overall system peaks. A resource that can be reliably dispatched at a particular location and time can potentially help address a specific distribution constraint.
Moving from the first model to the second requires closer coordination between utility planning departments, grid operators and customer-facing energy programs. It also requires utilities to rethink how they value distributed resources. Rather than treating them exclusively as customer-owned technologies or program participation numbers, utilities can begin evaluating their contribution to system capacity, reliability and operational flexibility.
Build Where Necessary. Optimize Wherever Possible
One of the biggest challenges in planning for commercial load growth is uncertainty. Large commercial projects may be announced years before they reach full operation, and development timelines, energy requirements and even project viability can change along the way.
That creates a difficult balancing act for utilities. Investing too early in infrastructure for demand that is delayed or never materializes can place unnecessary costs on the system. Waiting too long, however, can create capacity constraints that slow economic development and limit the ability to serve new customers.
A more adaptive approach allows utilities to align infrastructure investments with how demand actually develops. This may include phased upgrades, closer coordination with large commercial customers and the strategic use of flexible resources to manage constraints while longer-term infrastructure is planned and built. The objective is not to avoid new construction, but to make more informed decisions about where, when and how much capacity to add.
Every Megawatt Has to Work Harder
The shift toward commercial-led electricity demand growth is changing more than how much capacity utilities need. It is changing how they must evaluate and plan for that capacity.
As large loads emerge in concentrated locations and on uncertain timelines, the ability to distinguish between immediate constraints, future requirements and opportunities to use existing infrastructure more effectively will become increasingly important.
For utilities, the challenge is no longer simply preparing for more megawatts. It is making sure every investment, and every available megawatt, delivers the greatest possible value as demand evolves.
— Nick Tumilowicz is director of Product Management, Distributed Energy Management Solutions, at Itron.
