Uber Freight’s CEO has publicly come out with the company’s decision to no longer cooperate with Gartner when the technology and management advisory company does future work on the Magic Quadrant designation for Uber Freight.
Gartner’s latest interactions with Uber Freight (NYSE: UBER) over its annual ratings led CEO Rebecca Tinucci to take to LinkedIn and a company blog post to announce the company’s plans to end any cooperative efforts with Gartner on that widely-cited benchmark.
This was Tinucci’s first Gartner review since she became CEO at Uber Freight in August 2025.
In her LInkedIn post, Tinucci said she was “incredibly disappointed by this process and the only thing that’s clear is that this is not somewhere we’ll invest our time going forward. Back to focusing on our customers.”
A little less than a year ago, Gartner had a mixed rating on Uber Freight, putting it below the “cut line” on the “Ability to Execute” Y axis but past the X Axis cut line for the “Completeness of Vision” rating. To be in the Magic Quadrant, a company needs to be above the cut line for both categories, and be in the upper right hand corner of the four-square box: the magic quadrant..
The Magic Quadrant is that part of an X-Y axis box that has “ability to execute” and “completeness of vision” as its two measurements. A company that lands in the Magic Quadrant scores highly on both areas, and companies often tout to their customers, actual and potential, that they ended up in that sought-after space.
The Gartner webpage on its Magic Quadrant says it publishes 176 Magic Quadrant ratings each year.
Emails sent to Gartner had not been responded to by publication time. An Uber Freight spokeswoman declined further comment beyond Tinucci’s comments.
Taking on a giant
Getting into the Magic Quadrant and the ability to wear that as a badge of honor is what makes Tinucci’s public criticism so notable. Potential users of supply chain technology often look to Gartner’s commentary as a guide on what applications it should use. Publicly calling out the Gartner’s processes is a step that not many companies wish to take.
Tinucci wrote that Uber Freight had received its 2026 Fourth Party Logistics Magic Quadrant assessment, and asked for “the evidence behind our backward shift in positioning and consequential cautions.”
“We made it clear our concern was no longer our individual score,” Tinucci wrote. “The review started to feel like a negotiation over the assessment rather than an explanation of the evidence behind it.”
During the review of the score, Tinucci said Uber Freight felt the process was feeling more like a “negotiation” with Gartner (NYSE: IT) “rather than an explanation of the evidence behind it.”
Coming away with little confidence
“Our experience left us without confidence in the standards underpinning the report’s broader comparisons,” Tinucci said.
The company’s participation is presumably not necessary for Gartner to issue a rating. Tinucci said Uber Freight asked Gartner to no longer include its rating in the Magic Quadrant process, but Gartner declined.
“We are sharing our experience so customers and the industry can evaluate the research with that context,” Tinucci wrote.
Gartner does have a rating called Peer Insights. Tinucci said Uber Freight will continue to participate in that process, and she said the company currently has a rating of 4.6 out of 5.
Tinucci offered specifics on what she said were Uber Freight’s criticisms with the Gartner process.
An unidentified analyst from Gartner, according to Tinucci, “contacted our team outside the formal review channel and asked what it would take to get Uber Freight ‘across the finish line.’”
“That analyst raised the possibility of changing scores and removing a caution before Gartner’s authors could explain how they reached the original conclusions,” she wrote.
Trade article an issue
Tinucci said other points made by the Gartner analyst included concern over what the research firm referred to as a “single speculative trade article” as the basis for one negative finding. “When challenged, Gartner proposed materially rewriting it without adequately explaining the basis for the original conclusion or the change,” Tinucci said.
She wrapped up the recap of the process that Uber Freight is objecting to by noting that the “most significant backward movement” in the Gartner rating of Uber Freight was its “Completeness of Vision.” But Tinucci added that “Gartner acknowledged that a reader could find that result difficult to reconcile, that they “probably needed to go back and investigate.”
FourKites had its issues in the past
The sort of public break with Gartner, while rare, is not unprecedented.
In February 2025, supply chain technology leader FourKites said it would withdraw from the Magic Quadrant process. But its withdrawal did not come with the sort of criticism heard from Tinucci.
Instead, FourKites said it was withdrawing because of “the need to prioritize breakthrough AI innovations using Real-time Transportation Visibility Platform that are fundamentally reshaping supply chain operations.”
In a prepared statement released at the time, FourKites described Gartner’s RTTVP models as “not yet (accounting) for our innovation and roadmap.”

The Pacific Maritime Association and International Longshore and Warehouse Union Local 26 reached a tentative contract agreement early Saturday, easing the threat of a strike at six terminals at the Ports of Los Angeles and Long Beach. The deal covers roughly 250 unarmed security workers known as watchmen and still needs approval from Local 26 members. The current contract will stay in effect until the ratification vote.
What’s Related
“We thank the Federal Mediation and Conciliation Service and U.S. Department of Labor for their help, and the Local 26 bargaining committee for its work at the table,” the PMA said in a social media post. “This agreement provides certainty for the ports, for the cargo owners and workers throughout the supply chain who depend on them, and for the Southern California, regional and national economies .”
The danger of a strike
The watchmen make up about 2% of the ILWU workforce at Los Angeles and Long Beach, according to the PMA. But the six terminals where they work handle more than half of the two ports’ combined cargo, including roughly 85% of Long Beach’s volume and 33% of Los Angeles’ volume, the employer group estimates.
Dockworkers and marine clerks are covered by separate contracts. The PMA said it expected those workers to honor Local 26 picket lines, which could have halted ship loading and unloading and cut off truck access at affected terminals. The coastwide agreement covering about 22,000 longshore workers at 29 West Coast ports runs through 2028.
RELATED: Top 30 U.S. Ports Ranked By Container Imports In 2025
Even a short stoppage could have added to existing delays. Jabari Watt, senior director of operations at freight forwarder Flexport, said Los Angeles and Long Beach accounted for 37% of U.S. imports in October. Before the deal, he pointed to a rail backlog at Los Angeles and said delays could continue after terminals reopened.
“As of November 18, nearly half the imports waiting on on-dock rail at Los Angeles had been there nine days or more,” Watt said. “In 2012, a clerks’ strike idled 10 of the 14 container terminals for eight days. However long a stoppage lasts, those containers will still be in line when the gates reopen, so the delays would outlast the strike itself.”
What led to the tentative deal
The watchmen’s previous agreement expired in July 2025, and members continued working under extensions. Local 26 members authorized a strike, and the deadline moved several times in November. The two sides agreed to another short extension on Nov. 18, giving negotiators more time before the Saturday deadline.
Before the deal, the PMA said its offer included a $3,200 one-time bonus per member and would raise average annual earnings for full-time watchmen from more than $170,000 to $198,000. The proposal also called for keeping fully employer-paid health care for active workers and retirees and raising annual pension benefits to as much as $93,200 for the longest-serving workers.

The FDA approval of Wilserdly—the first new hormone therapy option for patients with early-stage breast cancer in more than 20 years—is the second straight greenlight for Roche’s drug, which got the nod for an advanced breast cancer subtype last week.
The FDA greenlit Roche’s Wilserdly Sunday as the first new hormone therapy for early-stage breast cancer in more than two decades—marking the drug’s second approval in just seven days.
The latest approval of Wilserdly—which was granted to Roche’s Genentech—allows the oral selective estrogen receptor degrader (SERD) to be used alone post-surgery in adult patients with estrogen receptor (ER)-positive, HER2-negative breast cancer. This is the most common subtype of the disease, accounting for around 70% of cases, according to the FDA’s announcement .
This follows last week’s approval for the aptly named Wilserdly—the drug’s first FDA greenlight—to treat second-line ER-positive, ESR1-mutated advanced breast cancer when combined with the mTOR inhibitor everolimus.
Wilserdly is the first and only SERD to be approved by the FDA in both early-stage and advanced ER-positive breast cancer, Roche said in a press release on Sunday.
The new FDA nod was backed by data from the Phase 3 lidERA study , in which Wilserdly—also known as giredestrant—reduced the risk of invasive disease recurrence or death by 30% versus standard of care endocrine therapy, meeting the trial’s primary endpoint. This result made Wilserdly the first oral estrogen receptor antagonist to show a benefit in early-stage breast cancer, the FDA said.
In lidERA, 4,170 patients with estrogen receptor-positive, HER2-negative breast cancer at intermediate to high risk of recurrence were given either Wilserdly or standard of care hormone therapy—tamoxifen or an aromatase inhibitor—for up to five years. At three years, 92.4% of patients taking Wilserdly were alive and free of invasive breast cancer compared to 89.6% of those on standard hormone therapy. Wilserdly-treated patients also had a lower risk of cancer returning in another part of the body, according to the FDA.
Roche is continuing to monitor patients to determine whether the treatment extends survival—a secondary endpoint of the trial—as a post-marketing commitment.
Wilserdly demonstrated a favorable safety profile, Roche said. The most common side effects, which occurred in at least 10% of trial participants, included muscle and joint pain, hot flashes, tiredness, headache, nausea and slower-than-normal heart rate. The FDA warned in its announcement that the drug may harm a developing baby if taken during pregnancy and that pre-menopausal women should take an additional hormone-suppressing medicine along with Wilserdly.
Meanwhile, last week’s approval in advanced breast cancer was supported by the evERA Breast Cancer study, in which Wilserdly combined with everolimus met the primary endpoint, significantly prolonging progression-free survival (PFS), the company said in its press release. In evERA, which included 373 patients, the Wilserdly combo led to a more than three-month PFS benefit, at 8.8 months versus 5.5 months with standard endocrine therapy plus everolimus.
It hasn’t all been smooth sailing for Wilserdly, however. In March, the asset failed to improve PFS in the Phase 3 persevERA Breast Cancer study, which was evaluating giredestrant plus palbociclib for people with ER-positive, HER2-negative, locally advanced or metastatic breast cancer in the first line setting. Roche fell 5% on the news.
Roche Pharmaceuticals CEO Teresa Graham has high hopes for Wilserdly. On a call with journalists, Graham said the drug has the potential to become the most successful in the company’s history, according to a Tuesday report by Reuters .
Without providing exact estimates, the executive said she expects Wilserdly’s peak sales to be similar to those of its current top-seller, multiple sclerosis drug Ocrevus, which generated $8.3 billion in 2025.

The Army's "Odin" tactical planning app can turn map data into a color-coded overlay of traversable terrain, no-go zones, and obstacles. (US Army DEVCOM C5ISR Center photo)
FORT BELVOIR, Va. — A team at the Army’s C5ISR Center on Fort Belvoir, Va., is working on a project dubbed Odin, which could be the service’s new AI-enhanced mission planning app for tactical units.
“We found that there was a gap in the Army at the tactical level,” Maj. Andrew Durfee, who heads the Odin team, said in a interview with Breaking Defense. “There’s robust mission planning capabilities at the division and the corps levels, [but] the farther that you get to that forward line of troops — what a lot of people reference as the ‘tactical edge’ — you have minimized compute, you have minimized bandwidth.”
Software optimized for brigades and above, where large staffs have bulky generators to power an arsenal of laptops, routers and servers, doesn’t necessarily translate to battalion and below, where a handful of officers and non-commissioned officers have to sketch out plans using militarized tablets and smartphones, he explained.
“Odin was created to basically bridge that gap … at the battalion, company and platoon level,” Durfee said.
Odin is now being integrated into the Army’s official battle network program, Next Generation Command and Control (NGC2), under a kind of “app store” or “ecosystem” approach to incorporating innovative software tools from non-traditional sources.
“We’ve done a tremendous amount of work with both Palantir and Anduril ,” Durfee said, particularly on smoothly sharing data. Earlier versions of the software were field-tested by the 4th Infantry Division and other units, including at this summer’s Project Convergence Capstone 6 (PCC-6) exercise, providing both positive feedback and critique to drive improvements.
“Over the last year we have had significant increase in capabilities,” Durfee said. Next year, the team aims to test the latest upgrades at PCC-7, roll out an official Minimum Viable Capability Release , and then hand over a mature version of Odin to the Army’s portfolio acquisition executive (PAE) for command and control systems.
While the developers keep adding features, Odin at its core is a way to automate planning processes traditionally done on paper — or, in some cases, Durfee recalls, drawn on the back of a used MRE ration box.
As a young officer, Durfee said, he often found himself “frantically writing down notes” while his superiors outlined a complex plan over the radio. Other times he’d wait for a courier from higher headquarters to arrive with a print-out or even hand-drawn diagrams of where to maneuver.
Odin allows frontline troops to exchange those detailed orders and map graphics electronically. It also taps into larger Army command networks — that’s where the collaboration with Anduril and Palantir comes in — to pull down data and automatically update the situation maps accordingly. That allows commanders to answer pressing tactical questions at a glance, instead of trying to make multiple radio calls and pull the details together in their head.
“Where is the enemy? Where are my friendly forces?” Durfee said. “What does the weather look like? Where are my sensors? What is the [intelligence] collection plan looking like?”
Odin can even help users visualize the “fog of war” by showing them the regions on the map where no friendly unit can see — either because it’s too far or blocked by an obstacle — which highlights gaps in their awareness where enemies might lurk unseen.
“We’ve seen this be very effective at PCC-6,” Durfee said, where one unit used the fog-of-war map to figure out which routes risked an ambush and which were safe to take. Now the team is working to add similar “where we can see/where we can’t” mapping for infrared sensors, radar and radio transmissions.
The team’s biggest ambition is to build what they call a “course of action generator,” using AI to help suggest everything from safe routes to entire schemes of maneuver. That goal’s beyond what the Fort Belvoir team can do itself, Durfee acknowledges, and it’ll be a challenge to get such complex software — which other military branches have experimented with — to run on the modest hardware a junior officer can carry into combat.
“We’re doing a heavy involvement with industry because … [these capabilities] require a robust amount of processing, compute power,” Durfee said. For now, he said, “we’re building a very light version.”

Trump does an ad for Tesla
President Trump says he “protected” Elon Musk during his first term, and that “you wouldn’t have Elon if it wasn’t for me.” He tied it to “a certain incident” that he called “a tough incident,” but he didn’t say what it was.
Musk had plenty of run-ins with federal regulators between 2017 and 2021. One of them could have ended his career as a public company CEO, and it’s our best guess.
Trump’s full quote
Trump called in to CNBC’s Squawk on the Street on Monday. That same morning, Nvidia’s board voted to reinstate Jensen Huang as CEO, and in its press release it said it had “received input from senior levels of the United States government” before concluding Huang posed no national security risk.
Trump argued that the US needs to “protect our geniuses.” Then he brought up Musk:
Advertisement - scroll for more content
“You know, I protected Elon in my first term. Very big. Elon was protected. I talk about it, and I’m proud of Elon. I love Elon. I think he’s great. You know, 80% super genius, 20% he has other problems. But I tell him that. But Elon, I protected. You wouldn’t have Elon if it wasn’t for me. And, you know, a certain incident took place, which was, you know, a tough incident.”
It’s not the first time he has hinted at it. Last week, in a Fox News interview from Shenzhen, Trump said: “I helped Elon a lot in my first term. I helped him a lot. He was in big trouble.” Back in 2024, he told CNBC he had helped Musk “when I was president,” again without details.
So what was the big trouble?
The prime suspect: ‘funding secured’
On August 7, 2018, Musk tweeted that he was “considering taking Tesla private at $420. Funding secured.” It wasn’t. Saudi Arabia’s Public Investment Fund had shown interest, but no deal or price had been agreed, and the take-private plan was dead within three weeks.
The SEC sued Musk for securities fraud on September 27, 2018. The agency didn’t only ask for a fine. It asked the court to bar Musk from serving as an officer or director of any public company. That would have meant no more Elon at Tesla, which lines up with “you wouldn’t have Elon if it wasn’t for me” better than anything else on this list.
And then it went away fast. Two days later, the SEC announced a settlement : Musk stayed CEO, gave up the chairman title for three years, and he and Tesla each paid $20 million, $40 million in total. Tesla added two independent directors and agreed to have a lawyer pre-approve Musk’s material tweets, but the SEC never fully enforced it. Musk didn’t admit or deny anything.
The SEC was run at the time by Jay Clayton, a Trump appointee.
There was a criminal side too. In September 2018, federal prosecutors in San Francisco opened a fraud investigation over the same tweet. It never led to charges, and the Justice Department never said publicly why.
The other candidates
The SEC came back in February 2019 and asked a judge to hold Musk in contempt after he tweeted Tesla production guidance without pre-approval. That one ended in April with an amended deal listing the topics he needed approval for, and no new penalty.
In May 2020, Musk reopened the Fremont factory in defiance of Alameda County’s COVID orders and tweeted: “If anyone is arrested, I ask that it only be me.” Trump tweeted the next day that California “should let Tesla & @elonmusk open the plant, NOW.” But the county was already working toward a reopening date of May 18, and a president doesn’t control county health orders.
There’s also the September 2018 Joe Rogan episode, where Musk smoked a joint on camera. NASA followed with a workplace safety review of SpaceX and Boeing, and SpaceX lives on federal contracts.
For context, Musk sat on Trump’s business advisory councils early in that first term, and quit in June 2017 when Trump pulled out of the Paris Agreement. That feels like a lifetime ago now that xAI runs its data centers on natural gas turbines.
Electrek’s Take
Our money is on “funding secured.”
Musk announced a take-private deal at a specific price that the other side never agreed to, and the stock jumped. It’s textbook securities fraud. The SEC asked to remove him from public company leadership, and two days later he got a $20 million fine, an insignificant amount of money for him, and lost a mostly insignificant title. For someone who’s now worth hundreds of billions, that’s a slap on the wrist.
The main remedy was supposed to be independent oversight. Tesla gave the chair to Robyn Denholm, who had been on the board since 2014, and the board has done what Musk wanted ever since: it defended his pay packages, approved new ones, and stayed quiet while the brand took damage. Denholm herself has sold tens of millions of dollars in TSLA along the way. The SEC got a governance fix on paper and nothing in practice.
Trump likes to take credit, and he could be inflating his role here. But if the White House leaned on the SEC or the Justice Department in 2018 to help a CEO facing fraud allegations, that’s a serious problem, and someone should look into it.
The timing doesn’t help. He said it the same day he appears to have intervened to reinstate Huang as CEO of Nvidia.
So what exactly did the administration do in 2018, and what does Musk owe for it?
